description:
We’re a multidisciplinary team of three: Matías, an aerospace engineering student; Nicolás, a computer science student; and Agustín, with a background in Business Administration.

We chose to work on an agriculture challenge because it brings together what we enjoy most: solving real problems, combining technology with research, and building something useful from different perspectives.

Engineering, technology and business — all working on the same problem.
summary:
Chacra is a web app that brings soil-care knowledge to each individual field. Pampas soils in Argentina have lost about 27% of their organic matter. Research institutions such as INTA and universities already know why and how to reverse it, but that knowledge stays in PDFs and WhatsApp groups, and farmers choose crops by price.

Chacra crosses published agronomic rules with NASA data for each field (NASA POWER, GPM, SMAP) and delivers it to the farmer as:

Alerts: what is happening, why (with source and date) and what you can do.
Season plan: your rotation compared with three alternatives over 25 years of NASA climate, weighted by income, water or soil.
AI assistant: answers in plain language and cites every number.
Marketplace: research rules, data layers, seeds and contractors nearby.

It addresses Field Shift by turning Earth observation data into concrete rotation choices: options, not orders. It matters because every farmer and institution that joins improves the next alert, protecting soil and income together.
details:
What it does. Chacra lets a farmer draw their field on a map and get three things: alerts (what is happening, why, with source and date, and what they can do), a season plan that compares their current crop rotation against alternatives, and an assistant that explains each number in plain language. A marketplace lists research rules, data layers, seeds and contractors. The pilot region is Villa María, Córdoba, Argentina.

How it works. A Python engine pulls weather history from NASA POWER (1981 to today), soil moisture from SMAP L4, rain from GPM IMERG, vegetation from MODIS and HLS, and terrain from SRTM, plus SoilGrids soil data, NOAA station records and Argentine crop statistics. It computes reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith) and a daily soil water balance for each rotation, then reports income (as illustrative values), water use, bare-soil days, nitrogen, erosion and yield ranges (p10/p50/p90). Agronomic rules published by research institutions trigger the alerts. The farmer sets what matters most (income, water or soil) and the ranking updates.

Benefits and impact. Farmers see the long-term cost of a rotation before sowing, not after. Advisors get traceable numbers to discuss. Research institutions reach thousands of fields at once and receive field data back. The intended impact is fewer months of bare soil, more diverse rotations and recovery of soil organic matter, without lowering income.

Tools. Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, MapLibre GL, zod, SWR; tested with Vitest and Playwright; deployed on Netlify. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Shapely, Google Earth Engine API. Interface in Spanish and English.

Creativity. Chacra does not build one more model nobody uses. It treats existing research as the product and NASA data as the trigger that makes it relevant to one field on one day. It gives options, not orders: the decision always stays with the farmer. It is also a network, where every farmer and institution that joins improves the next alert.

Factors considered. We interviewed advisors, farmers and researchers: data is scattered, complex tools go unused, and people want choices. So we prioritised plain vocabulary, mobile use in the field, and three levels of detail. Every value carries its source and date; missing data is shown as missing, never filled in. Model parameters are labelled as sourced, unverified or assumption. We validated predictions out of sample against weather stations and a naive baseline, and report failures as failures. We also documented known limits: NASA POWER grid cells smooth storms and frost.
